title: Conceptual Models of Abnormality
summary: The six main models used to explain and treat abnormal behaviour: biological, psychodynamic, behavioural, cognitive, humanistic-existential and socio-cultural, with their strengths and blind spots.

lesson.title: Different lenses, one child
lesson.hook: Seven-year-old Tobi screams, bites and cannot sit still in class. A doctor suspects brain chemistry, a pastor suspects spiritual attack, a teacher blames the home, a psychologist asks what the outbursts get him. Who is right?

slides.heading: What a model is
slides.body:
In science, a **model** (or **paradigm**) is the perspective used to explain a phenomenon. It sets out the scientist's **basic assumptions**, **gives order** to the field, and **guides investigation**: what to observe, which questions to ask, and how to interpret answers.

In abnormal psychology, several models compete to explain and treat disorders, including those of children.

terms.meaning: Behaviour and how it is learned
Effects of family, society and culture

slides.heading: No model is complete
slides.body:
The **biological** model sits at one end (the body), the **socio-cultural** model at the other (society). The four in between, **psychodynamic, behavioural, cognitive** and **humanistic-existential**, focus on psychological and personal functioning.

Each model highlights **one aspect** of human functioning. **None** can explain all abnormality alone, which is why modern clinicians combine them.

slides.question: Which model concentrates on the thinking that underlies behaviour?
slides.why: The cognitive model focuses on thought; the behavioural model on learned behaviour.

slides.heading: The biological model
slides.body:
Biological theorists take a **medical** view: abnormal behaviour is an **illness** caused by malfunctioning parts of the body, especially the **brain's anatomy or chemistry**.

Many disorders are linked to faulty **neurotransmission**. Some **anxiety disorders** are linked to **low GABA** activity; **schizophrenia** is linked mainly to **excess dopamine** activity. (Your course notes mention serotonin and norepinephrine here; dopamine is the classic link.)

slides.heading: Hormones and stress
slides.body:
The **endocrine system** works with neurons to control growth, reproduction, heart rate, temperature, energy and the **stress response**. Glands release **hormones** into the blood.

Under stress, the **adrenal glands** on top of the kidneys release **cortisol**. Abnormal cortisol secretion has been tied to **anxiety and mood disorders**. Head injury, poor **nutrition** and **vascular** disease can also disrupt brain function.

steps.title: Genetics
steps.detail: Inherited genes contribute strongly to schizophrenia, mood disorders and intellectual disability.

steps.title: Evolution
steps.detail: Some risk genes persisted because they once helped survival, such as strong fear responses to danger.

steps.title: Viral infections
steps.detail: Exposure to certain viruses before birth has been linked to schizophrenia and other disorders.

slides.heading: The cautious ancestor
slides.story: Imagine two ancestors walking through long grass. One startles at every rustle; the other strolls calmly. When a snake strikes, the jumpy one survives and passes on their genes. Today, a child who inherits that sensitive fear system may develop an anxiety disorder in a world with far fewer snakes.
slides.takeaway: Evolutionary theorists argue some genes behind disorders persisted because they once helped survival.

slides.question: Low activity of which neurotransmitter has been linked to some anxiety disorders?
slides.why: Low GABA activity is linked to anxiety. Cortisol and melatonin are hormones, not neurotransmitters.

slides.heading: How your lecturer will ask this
slides.body: Expect 'define models' and 'list the six models of abnormality', often as matching: model to focus. For the biological model, know neurotransmitters, hormones and the three sources: genetics, evolution, viral infections. Trap: calling cortisol a neurotransmitter. It is a hormone from the adrenal glands.
slides.sampleQuestion: Match each model with its focus: biological, socio-cultural, psychodynamic, behavioural, cognitive, humanistic-existential.
slides.howToAnswer: Biological: physical processes; socio-cultural: society and culture; psychodynamic: unconscious conflicts; behavioural: learned behaviour; cognitive: thinking; humanistic-existential: values and choices.

points: A model sets assumptions, orders a field and guides investigation.
Six models: biological, psychodynamic, behavioural, cognitive, humanistic-existential, socio-cultural.
No model explains all abnormality alone.
Biological: brain anatomy and chemistry, hormones like cortisol.
Sources: genetics, evolution, viral infections.

questions.stem: A scientific perspective that sets out assumptions and guides research on a phenomenon is called a:
questions.explanation: Models, also called paradigms, guide how scientists explain phenomena.

questions.stem: The biological model views abnormal behaviour mainly as:
options: An illness caused by malfunctioning body parts
questions.explanation: It takes a medical view centred on the brain and body.

questions.stem: Which model examines the effects of society and culture on behaviour?
questions.explanation: The socio-cultural model looks outwards to social forces.

questions.stem: During stress, the adrenal glands secrete:
questions.explanation: Cortisol is the adrenal stress hormone.

questions.stem: The three sources of biological abnormality identified are:
questions.explanation: Genetics, evolution and viral infections are the three sources.

questions.stem: Why do clinicians often combine models?
options: Each focuses on one aspect, and none explains all abnormality
questions.explanation: Combining models captures more of the whole picture.

questions.stem: A researcher finds a child's anxiety is linked to low GABA activity. This researcher is working within the:
questions.explanation: Neurotransmitter explanations belong to the biological model.

questions.stem: Studies linking schizophrenia to virus exposure before birth illustrate which biological source?
questions.explanation: Prenatal viral exposure is the viral-infection source.

questions.stem: A theorist argues that children's strong fear responses persist because they helped ancestors survive danger. This is an explanation from:
questions.explanation: Evolutionary theorists explain inherited traits by their past survival value.

questions.stem: All of the following are psychological models lying between the biological and socio-cultural models EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: 'Endocrine' refers to the hormone system, part of biology, not a model.

questions.stem: Excess activity of which neurotransmitter is most classically linked to schizophrenia?
questions.explanation: The dopamine hypothesis is the classic biochemical account of schizophrenia.

questions.stem: Which pair is correctly matched?
questions.explanation: The cognitive model focuses on thinking.

questions.stem: I. A model guides which questions a scientist asks. II. The biological model explains all abnormality. III. Abnormal cortisol has been tied to anxiety and mood disorders. Which are correct?
questions.explanation: I and III are correct. No single model, biological included, explains all abnormality.

questions.stem: A child develops behaviour problems after a head injury in a road accident. Which model offers the most direct explanation?
questions.explanation: Head injury causing brain dysfunction is a biological explanation.

questions.stem: Why do critics say the biological model alone may be insufficient for childhood disorders?
options: It can overlook family, learning and cultural influences that also shape behaviour
questions.explanation: Focusing only on biology misses psychological and social factors.

lesson.title: Hidden forces in the mind
lesson.hook: A child who was neglected as a baby grows into a teenager who clings to every friend and panics when left alone. Freud would say something from those first months is still at work, out of sight.

slides.heading: Underlying psychological forces
slides.body:
Psychodynamic theorists believe behaviour, normal or abnormal, is driven by **psychological forces** we are **not consciously aware of**. These forces are **dynamic**: they interact, and their interaction produces behaviour, thoughts and emotions.

Abnormal symptoms are seen as the result of **conflicts** between these forces.

slides.heading: Freud and psychoanalysis
slides.body:
**Sigmund Freud** (1856–1939), a neurologist in Vienna, created this model around 1900. He developed **psychoanalysis** to explain both normal and abnormal functioning.

Freud proposed three central forces shaping personality: **instinctual needs**, **rational thinking** and **moral standards**. He called them the **id**, **ego** and **superego**.

left.title: Id
points: Instinctual needs and drives
Pleasure principle: wants gratification now
Fuelled by libido

right.title: Ego
points: Separates off from the id
Reality principle: when it is safe to act
Uses defence mechanisms

slides.heading: The superego
slides.body:
The **superego** grows from the ego. As children learn from parents that many id impulses are unacceptable, they **introject** (absorb) their parents' values. They identify with their parents and judge themselves by those standards.

The result is a **conscience**: we feel good when we live up to these values and **guilty** when we break them.

slides.question: The part of personality that operates on the pleasure principle is the:
slides.why: The id seeks immediate gratification. The ego follows the reality principle.

slides.heading: Healthy balance and conflict
slides.body:
The id, ego and superego are usually in **some conflict**. A **healthy** personality has an effective working relationship, an acceptable **compromise**, among the three.

When conflict is **excessive**, behaviour may show signs of **dysfunction**. To cope, the ego uses **defence mechanisms** such as **repression, denial, projection, rationalisation, displacement, regression** and **sublimation**.

steps.title: Oral (0 to 18 months)
steps.detail: Pleasure centres on the mouth: feeding and sucking.

steps.title: Anal (18 months to 3 years)
steps.detail: Focus on toilet training and control.

steps.title: Phallic (3 to 5 or 6 years)
steps.detail: Focus on the genitals and identification with parents.

steps.title: Latency (about 6 to 12)
steps.detail: Sexual interests quieten; school and friendships dominate.

slides.heading: Fixation
slides.body:
At each stage, new pressures require the id, ego and superego to adjust. Successful adjustment brings **growth**. If not, the person may become **fixated** at that stage, and later development suffers.

Because **parents** are the key figures in early life, they are often seen as the source of problems. A child whose **oral needs** are consistently unmet may become fixated orally, showing **extreme dependence or mistrust** and a higher risk of **depression**.

slides.question: According to Freud, the latency stage covers roughly:
slides.why: Latency falls between the phallic stage and puberty, roughly ages 6 to 12, when sexual interests quieten.

slides.heading: The new baby
slides.story: When her baby brother arrives, five-year-old Kemi, who had been toilet-trained for two years, starts wetting the bed and asking for a feeding bottle. A psychodynamic therapist would see regression: under the stress of losing her parents' full attention, Kemi's ego retreats to an earlier, safer stage.
slides.takeaway: Defence mechanisms like regression protect the ego from anxiety, especially in children under stress.

slides.heading: How your lecturer will ask this
slides.body: Expect 'explain the psychodynamic model' with id, ego, superego, the principles they follow, and fixation. Objectives test stage ages and defence mechanisms with child scenarios. Traps: saying the ego follows the pleasure principle (it follows reality), and forgetting that the superego develops from the ego.
slides.sampleQuestion: A child whose mother consistently failed to meet her feeding needs becomes extremely dependent. Freud would describe this as fixation at the: (a) anal stage (b) oral stage (c) phallic stage (d) genital stage
slides.howToAnswer: Answer (b). Explain fixation and link oral fixation to dependence, mistrust and vulnerability to depression.

points: Behaviour is driven by unconscious, interacting forces; symptoms reflect conflict.
Freud: id (pleasure principle), ego (reality principle), superego (conscience).
Healthy personality is a workable compromise among the three.
Defence mechanisms protect the ego from anxiety.
Unresolved stages cause fixation; oral fixation links to dependence and depression.

questions.stem: The psychodynamic model was first formulated by:
questions.explanation: Freud developed psychoanalysis, the basis of the psychodynamic model.

questions.stem: The ego operates according to the:
questions.explanation: The ego seeks gratification realistically, following the reality principle.

questions.stem: The conscience is part of the:
questions.explanation: The superego contains internalised moral standards, the conscience.

questions.stem: According to Freud, the oral stage covers roughly:
questions.explanation: The oral stage spans the first 18 months.

questions.stem: The ego develops strategies to control unacceptable id impulses called:
questions.explanation: Defence mechanisms reduce anxiety from unacceptable impulses.

questions.stem: The superego develops when children:
questions.explanation: Absorbing parents' values forms the conscience.

questions.stem: A boy who is angry at his teacher goes home and kicks his younger brother. This defence mechanism is:
questions.explanation: Redirecting feelings to a safer target is displacement.

questions.stem: A child who failed an exam insists the teacher set unfair questions, though classmates did well. This is most likely:
questions.explanation: Offering a plausible excuse to protect self-esteem is rationalisation.

questions.stem: A toddler grabs a sweet from a shop shelf the moment he sees it. Freud would say this impulse comes from the:
questions.explanation: Seeking immediate gratification reflects the id's pleasure principle.

questions.stem: Which ordering of Freud's stages is correct?
questions.explanation: The sequence is oral, anal, phallic, latency, genital.

questions.stem: According to the psychodynamic model, a healthy personality is one in which:
options: The id, ego and superego reach an acceptable compromise
There is no conflict at all
questions.explanation: Some conflict is normal; health means a workable compromise.

questions.stem: All of the following are defence mechanisms EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Introspection is self-examination, not a defence mechanism.

questions.stem: I. The id is fuelled by libido. II. The ego develops from the superego. III. Fixation can follow failed adjustment at a stage. Which are correct?
questions.explanation: I and III are correct. The ego separates off from the id; the superego grows from the ego.

questions.stem: Why are parents so central in psychodynamic explanations of childhood disorders?
options: They are the key environmental figures during the early stages when fixation can occur
questions.explanation: Early stages are shaped by parental care, so failures there are often traced to parents.

questions.stem: A major criticism of the psychodynamic model is that:
options: Its unconscious concepts are hard to test scientifically
It focuses only on brain chemistry
questions.explanation: Unconscious forces are difficult to observe or measure, limiting scientific testing.

lesson.title: Four more lenses
lesson.hook: A boy refuses to go to school. One psychologist asks what he gains by staying home; another asks what he believes will happen there; a third asks whether he feels his life has meaning; a fourth looks at bullying in his community. All four may find part of the answer.

slides.heading: The behavioural model
slides.body:
**Behaviourists** focus on **behaviour** and argue it develops through the **principles of learning**. Learned behaviours help us cope, but **abnormal behaviours can be learned too**.

Behavioural therapy aims to **identify** problem behaviours and **replace** them with more appropriate ones using learning principles. For example, **systematic desensitisation**, based on classical conditioning, treats **phobias** effectively.

terms.meaning: Learning that links two events because they keep happening at nearly the same moment
Learning to behave in ways that bring rewards
Learning by observing and copying others

slides.heading: The tantrum that works
slides.story: Every time four-year-old Bayo throws a tantrum at the supermarket, his embarrassed mother buys him biscuits to quieten him. Soon he throws a tantrum on every trip. A behaviour therapist teaches her to reward calm behaviour instead and ignore tantrums. Within weeks, they become rare.
slides.takeaway: Operant conditioning can teach problem behaviour, and the same principles can unlearn it.

slides.question: A child learns to fear dogs after watching his older sister scream at one. This is:
slides.why: Learning by observing someone else's reaction is modelling.

slides.heading: The cognitive model
slides.body:
The **cognitive model** holds that to understand behaviour, we must understand **thought**. Abnormal functioning comes from **cognitive problems**: **maladaptive assumptions** and **illogical thinking**.

**Cognitive therapists** help people **recognise and change** faulty ideas. A child who thinks 'If I get one answer wrong, everyone will laugh at me' can learn to test and revise that belief.

slides.heading: Humanistic-existential model
slides.body:
This model focuses on the human need to face **philosophical issues**: **self-awareness, values, meaning and choice**. **Humanists** believe people are driven to **self-actualise**; when that drive is blocked, abnormality may follow.

**Client-centred** therapists (Carl Rogers) create a warm, accepting climate for honest self-exploration. **Gestalt** therapists use more active techniques to help people recognise their needs.

slides.heading: The existential view
slides.body: For **existentialists**, abnormality grows when people **run away from the responsibilities of living**. Their therapists encourage people to **accept responsibility** for their lives, recognise their **freedom to choose** a different course, and live with greater **meaning**.

slides.heading: The socio-cultural model
slides.body:
This model turns its gaze **outwards**, to the social forces acting on people. **Family systems** theorists argue a family's structure or communication patterns can push members into abnormal behaviour. Others study **culture**, **social networks and support**, and **societal conditions** such as poverty.

**Labelling** theorists say that when society calls someone 'mentally ill', the **label itself** can shape how they behave and how others treat them.

slides.question: A theorist argues that calling a child 'the mad one' in his village changes how he behaves and how others treat him. This view comes from the:
slides.why: Concern with societal labels and roles belongs to the socio-cultural model.

slides.heading: How your lecturer will ask this
slides.body: Expect 'explain the various models of abnormality' as an essay: one paragraph per model with key idea, cause of abnormality and treatment. Objectives use child scenarios to identify the model. Trap: confusing client-centred (supportive, Rogers) with Gestalt (active techniques), or modelling with operant conditioning.
slides.sampleQuestion: Which model traces abnormality to people dodging the responsibilities of their own lives? (a) behavioural (b) cognitive (c) existential (d) socio-cultural
slides.howToAnswer: Answer (c). Then contrast with humanists, who stress blocked self-actualisation.

points: Behavioural: abnormal behaviour is learned through conditioning and modelling.
Cognitive: maladaptive assumptions and illogical thinking cause problems.
Humanistic: blocked self-actualisation; client-centred and Gestalt therapy.
Existential: hiding from responsibility; therapy restores choice and meaning.
Socio-cultural: family systems, culture, support and labels.

questions.stem: Behaviourists explain abnormal behaviour mainly through:
questions.explanation: Behaviourists see behaviour, normal or abnormal, as learned.

questions.stem: Humanists believe people are driven to:
questions.explanation: Self-actualisation is the central humanistic drive.

questions.stem: Systematic desensitisation is especially effective for treating:
questions.explanation: This classical-conditioning technique treats phobias well.

questions.stem: When a child links two events because they keep happening at nearly the same moment, the learning is called:
questions.explanation: Classical conditioning involves temporal association.

questions.stem: Cognitive theorists attribute abnormal functioning to:
questions.explanation: Faulty thinking is the cognitive model's explanation.

questions.stem: Client-centred therapists aim to:
options: Create a supportive climate for honest self-exploration
questions.explanation: Rogers' approach offers warmth and acceptance to foster self-actualisation.

questions.stem: A girl gets attention from her teacher only when she misbehaves, and her misbehaviour increases. This is best explained by:
questions.explanation: Behaviour followed by a reward (attention) increases: operant conditioning.

questions.stem: A therapist helps a child replace the thought 'I'm stupid at everything' with a more accurate view. This approach is:
questions.explanation: Changing faulty beliefs is cognitive therapy.

questions.stem: A family therapist notices a child's problems worsen whenever his parents argue through him. This reflects the:
options: Family systems view within the socio-cultural model
questions.explanation: Family structure and communication patterns are a socio-cultural focus.

questions.stem: All of the following are forms of conditioning in the behavioural model EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Introjection is a psychodynamic concept.

questions.stem: Which pair is correctly matched?
options: Existential therapy: accepting responsibility and choice
questions.explanation: Existential therapy stresses responsibility, freedom and meaning.

questions.stem: Labelling theorists in the socio-cultural model argue that:
options: Being labelled mentally ill can influence how a person behaves and is treated
questions.explanation: The label itself can shape behaviour and others' responses.

questions.stem: I. Abnormal behaviour can be learned. II. Gestalt therapists use active techniques. III. Existentialists see abnormality as hiding from responsibility. Which are correct?
questions.explanation: All three statements are correct.

questions.stem: A child's school refusal is linked to low serotonin, fearful beliefs, a reward of staying home, and bullying in the community. Which conclusion best fits?
options: Several models each explain part of the problem
questions.explanation: No single model explains everything; an integrated approach captures the whole picture.

questions.stem: Which model would most likely treat a child's phobia of the dark by gradually exposing them to dim light while they stay relaxed?
questions.explanation: Gradual exposure paired with relaxation is systematic desensitisation, a behavioural technique.
